decks.name: U3 Grammar · Comparatives and superlatives
decks.desc: Unit 3: Comparatives and superlatives. Short adjectives: add -er and the -est: cheap, cheaper, the cheapest. Watch the spelling: big, bigger; easy, easier. Long adjectives use more and the most: more difficult than, the most exciting. Irregular: good, better, the best; bad, worse, the worst; far, further, the furthest. Use than after a comparative, in after a superlative (the best in the class) and as ... as to say two things are equal.

decks.name: U5 Grammar · Past simple and past continuous
decks.desc: Unit 5: Past simple and past continuous. Past continuous is the longer action in progress. Past simple is the short action that interrupts it: I was having a shower when the phone rang. when usually goes before the past simple action: We were sleeping when the burglar came in. while usually goes before the past continuous action: While we were walking home, it started to rain.

decks.name: U7 Grammar · have to, must and should
decks.desc: Unit 7: have to, must and should. have to + infinitive means it is necessary, often a rule. It changes: has to, had to, Do you have to? must + infinitive without to also means it is necessary. It has no -s and no past form (use had to): I must phone Gran. mustn't means it is not allowed. don't have to means it is not necessary: You mustn't shout. You don't have to pay. should and shouldn't + infinitive give advice: You should say sorry.

decks.name: U8 Grammar · Comparative and superlative adjectives
decks.desc: Unit 8: Comparative and superlative adjectives. Short adjectives add -er and -est: tall, taller, the tallest. Spelling: large, larger; hot, hotter; easy, easier. Longer adjectives use more and the most: more expensive, the most expensive. less is the opposite of more. Irregular: good, better, the best; bad, worse, the worst; far, further, the furthest. Use than after comparatives and as + adjective + as to say things are equal: It isn't as new as yours.

decks.name: U9 Grammar · Future forms: present continuous, will, be going to and future continuous
decks.desc: Unit 9: Future forms: present continuous, will, be going to and future continuous. Present continuous + a time for fixed arrangements: I'm seeing the dentist at four. will + infinitive for predictions, offers and promises: I think robots will do more jobs. I'll carry that for you. be going to + infinitive for plans and intentions: We're going to paint my room this weekend. decks.name: U10 Grammar · Zero, first and second conditionals
decks.desc: Unit 10: Zero, first and second conditionals. Zero: if + present, present. For things that are always true: If you heat ice, it melts. First: if + present, will or won't + infinitive. For real future possibilities: If it rains, we'll stay at home. Second: if + past simple, would or wouldn't + infinitive. For unreal or unlikely situations: If I had a boat, I would sail to Ibiza. No will or would in the if-clause. unless means if not.

decks.name: U11 Grammar · Past perfect
decks.desc: Unit 11: Past perfect. Form: had + past participle, the same for all persons: I had left. She hadn't eaten. Had they arrived? Use it for an action that happened before another action or time in the past: When we got to the station, the train had gone. The later action is in the past simple; the earlier one is in the past perfect: I was hungry because I hadn't had breakfast.

decks.name: U12 Grammar · Modals of obligation, necessity and advice: should, need to, have to, needn'
decks.desc: Unit 12: Modals of obligation, necessity and advice: should, need to, have to, needn't. should and shouldn't + infinitive give advice: You should pack a jumper. need to + infinitive means it is important or necessary: You need to book early. It changes: she needs to, Do I need to? have to + infinitive means it is necessary because of a rule or law: You have to wear a seat belt. don't have to, don't need to and needn't (+ infinitive without to) mean it is not necessary: You needn't hurry.

decks.name: U13 Grammar · The passive: present, past and with modal verbs
decks.desc: Unit 13: The passive: present, past and with modal verbs. Passive is the verb be + past participle. Change be to show the tense. Present simple passive: am, is, are + participle. Use by for the person who does the action.

decks.name: U14 Grammar · Relative clauses: defining and non-defining
decks.desc: Unit 14: Relative clauses: defining and non-defining. Defining clauses say which person or thing we mean and have no commas: The boy who sits next to me is Italian. who for people, which for things, that for people or things, whose for possession, where for places. You can leave out who, which or that when it is the object: The film (that) we saw was great. Non-defining clauses add extra information between commas. Do not use that: My gran, who is eighty, still bakes.

decks.name: U17 Grammar · Reported questions

For yes/no questions use if or whether: 'Are you ready?' She asked if I was ready.

decks.name: U6 Grammar · Present perfect and past simple
decks.desc: Unit 6: Present perfect and past simple. Present perfect (have/has + past participle) links the past to now, and the time is not given: I've lost my keys. She's phoned three times this morning. Past simple for a finished time (yesterday, last week, in 2015, two days ago, when ...?): We ate out last night. just, already and never go before the participle; yet goes at the end of negatives and questions; still goes before hasn't or haven't.

decks.desc: Unit 7: Ability and possibility: can, could, be able to, managed to, may, might. Present ability: can or am/is/are able to. General ability in the past: could or was/were able to: My gran could speak three languages. For success on one occasion in the past use managed to or was/were able to, NOT could: The door was stuck, but we managed to open it. (couldn't is fine.) can has no infinitive, -ing form or participle, so use be able to: I'll be able to come. I've never been able to whistle.

decks.desc: Unit 8: Future plans: present simple, present continuous, be going to and will. Present simple for timetables: The museum opens at ten tomorrow. decks.name: U9 Grammar · Future predictions: be going to, will, may/might and future continuous
decks.desc: Unit 9: Future predictions: be going to, will, may/might and future continuous. be going to for predictions based on something you can see or know now: Look at those clouds. It's going to rain. will for predictions based on opinion, often with I think, I'm sure, probably: I think Brazil will win. may, might and could + infinitive when you are less sure: Prices might go up. Future continuous (will be + -ing) for an action in progress at a future time: This time next week I'll be lying on a beach.

decks.name: U10 Grammar · The passive
decks.desc: Unit 10: The passive. Form: the right tense of be + past participle: Coffee is grown in Brazil. The bridge was built in 1900. The hall is being cleaned. My bike has been stolen. After will and modal verbs use be + past participle: It will be finished tomorrow. It must be done. Use the passive when we don't know or don't care who does the action. Add by + agent only if it is important: This song was written by a teenager.

decks.name: U11 Grammar · Present perfect continuous
decks.desc: Unit 11: Present perfect continuous. Form: have/has been + -ing: I've been waiting. She hasn't been sleeping well. Have you been crying? Use it with for, since and how long to stress how long: We've been playing for two hours.

decks.name: U13 Grammar · Reported statements
decks.desc: Unit 13: Reported statements. After said or told, the tense usually moves one step back: 'I'm tired.' She said she was tired. 'I lost it.' She told me (that) she was busy.

decks.name: U3 Grammar · THE GRAMMAR OF PHRASAL VERBS

Verb + adverb + object: a noun object can go before or after the particle ('turn off the TV' / 'turn the TV off'), but a pronoun must go in the middle: 'turn it off'.

decks.name: U4 Grammar · MODALS (1): NECESSITY, OBLIGATION, PROHIBITION AND ADVICE

decks.name: U5 Grammar · PRESENT AND PAST HABITS
decks.desc: Unit 5: PRESENT AND PAST HABITS. Present habits: present simple + frequency adverb (before the main verb, after be) or a frequency phrase at the end. 'I hardly ever eat meat.' 'We meet from time to time.' always / constantly / continually + present continuous shows a habit annoys you: 'She's always borrowing my pens.' used to + infinitive: past habits and states that are no longer true. Negative and question: didn't use to / Did you use to ...?

decks.name: U6 Grammar · BE/GET USED TO
decks.desc: Unit 6: BE/GET USED TO. be used to + noun or -ing: something is normal for you now. 'I'm used to the noise.' get used to + noun or -ing: something is slowly becoming normal. 'I'm getting used to my new school.' Here 'to' is a preposition, so the next verb takes -ing: 'She's used to cooking for ten people.' (NOT 'used to cook') be and get can go in any tense: 'I wasn't used to it', 'You'll get used to it', 'He has got used to it'.

He has lived in Seville for years, so he ____ the heat. (is used to / used to) | is used to

Correct it: I'm not use to spicy food. | I'm not used to spicy food.
We ____ live in a flat, but now we have a house. (used to / are used to) | used to
She still hasn't ____ (get) used to her new timetable. | got
Are you used to ____ (speak) in public? | speaking

decks.name: U7 Grammar · NARRATIVE TENSES
decks.desc: Unit 7: NARRATIVE TENSES. Past simple tells the main events of a story in order: 'She opened the box and smiled.' Past continuous sets the scene or shows an action in progress: 'The wind was blowing hard.' Past perfect simple (had + past participle): a completed action before another past event. 'By the time we arrived, they had eaten.'

While they ____ (sleep), someone stole their car. | were sleeping
The ground was wet. It ____ (rain) all night. | had been raining

decks.name: U8 Grammar · FUTURE (1): REVIEW
decks.desc: Unit 8: FUTURE (1): REVIEW. Present simple for timetables and fixed schedules: 'My flight leaves at noon.' Present continuous for arrangements with other people: 'I'm seeing the dentist on Friday.' be going to: intentions already decided, and predictions from what you can see now. 'It's going to fall!' will: decisions made at the moment of speaking, offers, promises and predictions based on opinion. 'I'll carry that for you.'

decks.name: U9 Grammar · FUTURE (2): CONTINUOUS AND PERFECT
decks.desc: Unit 9: FUTURE (2): CONTINUOUS AND PERFECT. Future continuous (will be + -ing): an action in progress at a future moment. 'At ten tomorrow I'll be sitting my exam.' decks.name: U10 Grammar · MODALS (2): MODALS IN THE PAST

decks.name: U11 Grammar · RELATIVE CLAUSES

decks.name: U13 Grammar · THE PASSIVE (2): OTHER STRUCTURES
decks.desc: Unit 13: THE PASSIVE (2): OTHER STRUCTURES. Passive infinitive = (to) be + past participle. It follows verbs like want, hope, expect, seem: 'Everyone wants to be liked.' decks.name: U14 Grammar · REPORTED SPEECH
decks.desc: Unit 14: REPORTED SPEECH. Tenses usually move one step back (am - was, have done - had done, did - had done, will - would, can - could). The past perfect, would, could and should stay the same. The word that is optional. No tense change is needed if the words are still true or if the reporting verb is in the present: She says she's tired.
words: 'I'm hungry.' He said he ____ hungry. | was
'I'll help you.' She said she ____ help me. | would
'We've finished.' They said they ____ finished. | had
'I saw it yesterday.' He said he had seen it the day ____. | before
She suggested ____ a taxi. (to take / taking) | taking
He offered ____ me home. (to drive / driving) | to drive
He apologised ____ being late. (for / of / about) | for
Correct it: He said me the truth. | He told me the truth.
'I'll be here tomorrow.' He said he'd be ____ the next day. | there
The doctor advised me ____ (rest). | to rest
Tom denied ____ the window. (breaking / to break) | breaking
It ____ (say) that the castle is haunted. | is said

decks.name: U15 Grammar · RELATIVE CLAUSES
decks.desc: Unit 15: RELATIVE CLAUSES. who / that for people, which / that for things, whose for possession, where for places, when for times, why for reasons. whom is formal and used after prepositions. Defining clauses give essential information and have no commas. When the pronoun is the object of the clause you can drop it: The film (that) we saw was great.
words: The woman ____ lives next door is a vet. (who / which) | who
That's the boy ____ dog bit me. (one word) | whose
This is the town ____ I was born. (one word) | where
My mum, ____ is 50, runs marathons. (who / that) | who
Can 'that' be left out? The book that I bought was cheap. (yes / no) | yes
Correct it: The man which called was rude. | The man who called was rude.
I'll never forget the day ____ we met. (when / where) | when
He failed the test, ____ surprised everyone. (which / what) | which
Formal: The person to ____ I spoke was helpful. (one word) | whom
Correct it: Madrid, that is huge, is fun. | Madrid, which is huge, is fun.
That's the reason ____ I left early. (why / which) | why
Which type of relative clause needs commas? (defining / non-defining) | non-defining

decks.name: U16 Grammar · PARTICIPLE CLAUSES
decks.desc: Unit 16: PARTICIPLE CLAUSES. Present participle (-ing) clauses describe an action at the same time as, or just before, the main action, or its result: Opening the door, she saw a stranger. Both parts must share the same subject. They can follow conjunctions and prepositions such as while, after, before, since, on: After leaving school, he moved abroad.
words: ____ (walk) along the beach, I found a ring. | Walking
____ (finish) her homework first, she then went out. (perfect participle) | Having finished

She sat by the fire, ____ a book. (reading / read) | reading

After ____ (leave) school, he moved to London. | leaving
Correct it: Having ate, we went out. | Having eaten, we went out.
____ in simple English, the book is easy to read. (Written / Writing) | Written
